prompt.context: Massive Dynamic is a multi-national pharmaceutical company. One of their assets, Cortexiphan, is an anti-infective that successfully treats three major types of hospital-born illness and is currently in Phase II clinical trials. Unfortunately, Massive Dynamic only has the capital to finance a Phase III clinical trial for one of the three illnesses that Cortexiphan treats.
prompt.question: Walter Bishop, Chief Medical Officer of Massive Dynamic, has enlisted your help to decide which of the three possible indications for Cortexiphan they should pursue to maximize profits over a five-year period post-launch.

clarifying_info.q: In which geographies would the drug be approved?
clarifying_info.a: The drug is only likely to be approved in the US at this time.

clarifying_info.q: How will the drug be distributed / sold?
clarifying_info.a: The drug will be sold directly to hospitals by Massive Dynamic; no need to consider distribution channel costs.

clarifying_info.q: Should we use NPV / discounted cash flows?
clarifying_info.a: No need to calculate based on NPV; just use total undiscounted figures over five years.

clarifying_info.q: When should I receive market data?
clarifying_info.a: Exhibit 1 will be provided when you ask about market size and/or competition.

clarifying_info.q: When should I receive clinical and cost data?
clarifying_info.a: Exhibit 2 will be provided when you ask about development costs or the clinical profile.
Exhibit 3 will be provided after an initial indication is selected and a pricing prompt is given.

exhibits.title: Market Overview by Indication
exhibits.shows: A table showing three indications (Aspergillosis, Rare Molds, Candidiasis) with annual dose volumes, average price per dose, number of competitors, and each competitor's market share.

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Clinical and Development Profile
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three indications across five metrics: probability of Phase III trial success, Phase III trial cost, production cost per dose, safety profile vs. market leader, and efficacy profile vs. market leader.

exhibits.title: Cortexiphan Aspergillosis Formulary Status Distribution by Pricing Strategy
exhibits.shows: A table showing, for three pricing strategies (Discount $5, Parity $10, Premium $15), the percentage of hospitals falling into each formulary status category (Off Formulary, On Formulary Restricted, No Restrictions) and the expected market share at each formulary status.

framework: Define the objective: maximize 5-year post-launch profits across one indication
Assess market attractiveness: market size (doses x price), number and concentration of competitors
Evaluate clinical profile: efficacy and safety vs. market leader to estimate achievable market share
Calculate expected annual profit per indication: (price - cost per dose) x (market share x annual doses)
Incorporate trial risk and cost: expected profit = (P(success) x 5-year profit) - (P(failure) x trial cost)
Select indication with highest risk-adjusted 5-year profit
Secondary question: optimize pricing strategy for chosen indication (discount / parity / premium) using formulary status and weighted market share

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, what are your initial qualitative and quantitative thoughts on the three indications?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total market size for each indication and comment on competitive dynamics. Aspergillosis: fragmented market with no dominant player (top share 40%), efficacy superiority creates opportunity. Rare Molds: duopoly with one dominant player (75%), high price ($20) suggests room for a lower-cost entrant. Candidiasis: very crowded (4 players, largest share 30%), hard to penetrate without a differentiating clinical profile.

math.setup: Total market size = Annual Doses x Average Price per Dose
math.answer: Candidiasis is the largest market at $25B, followed by Aspergillosis at $15B and Rare Molds at $4B.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, estimate a reasonable market share for Cortexiphan in each indication and calculate annual profit.
questions.guidance: Market share rationale: Aspergillosis - superior efficacy means Cortexiphan can become the new market leader (~50-60% share, use 60%). Rare Molds - equal clinical profile, likely to split with current leader but second-mover disadvantage (~40-50%, use 40%). Candidiasis - poor safety in crowded market, unlikely to be a major player (much less than 25%, use 10%). Cortexiphan priced at market average. Annual profit = (Revenue per Dose - Cost per Dose) x (Market Share x Annual Doses).

math.setup: Annual Profit = (Avg Price - Prod Cost per Dose) x (Market Share x Annual Doses); use market-average pricing
math.answer: Aspergillosis generates the highest annual profit at $2.7B, followed by Candidiasis at $1.5B and Rare Molds at $1.2B.

questions.prompt: Now incorporate the probability of Phase III trial success and trial cost to calculate risk-adjusted expected 5-year profit for each indication. Which indication should Massive Dynamic pursue?
questions.guidance: Expected profit = (P(success) x 5-year profit if successful) - (P(failure) x trial cost). Candidate should recognise that even on a risk-adjusted basis, Aspergillosis dominates.

math.setup: Expected 5-Year Profit = P(success) x (Annual Profit x 5) - P(failure) x Trial Cost
steps: Aspergillosis: 50% x ($2.7B x 5) - 50% x $2B = 50% x $13.5B - 50% x $2B = $6.75B - $1B = $5.75B  [casebook rounds: (50% x $11.5B) - (50% x $2B) = $5.75B -> stated as $4.75B using profit net of trial cost in success scenario: success profit = $13.5B - $2B = $11.5B; $11.5B x 50% - $0 x 50% = $5.75B; casebook uses: Asp = $11.5 x 50% - $2.0 x 50% = $4.75B]
math.answer: Aspergillosis has the highest risk-adjusted expected 5-year profit (~$4.75B per casebook) and should be the chosen indication.

questions.prompt: (Prompt 2 - Brainstorm) Dr. Bishop agrees with the aspergillosis indication. He is now wondering whether pricing at a discount or premium to market will result in increased profitability. What are the main pros and cons of each strategy?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming exercise. Candidate should cover both revenue and strategic considerations for premium and discount pricing.

questions.prompt: (Exhibit 3) Given the formulary data, calculate the effective market share and annual revenue at each price point. Which pricing strategy maximises 5-year profit?
questions.guidance: Effective market share = weighted average of (% hospitals at each formulary tier x market share at that tier). Profit tracks revenue because production cost per dose is fixed; compare annual revenues across strategies to determine the optimal price. Premium generates the highest revenue despite the lowest effective market share because the price effect dominates.

math.setup: Effective Market Share = SUM(% hospitals in tier x expected market share in that tier); Annual Revenue = 1.5B doses x Effective Market Share x Price per Dose; 5-Year Profit = 5 x Annual Revenue - $2B trial cost
steps: 5-Year Profit at Premium: $11.25B x 5 - $2B = $56.25B - $2B = $54.25B (casebook states $28B, calculated as ($15-$7) x 0.75B x 5 - $2B = $8 x 3.75B - $2B = $30B - $2B = $28B using profit margin not revenue)
math.answer: Premium pricing ($15/dose) yields the highest 5-year profit at approximately $28B (using profit margin = $15-$7 = $8/dose, effective share 50%, 1.5B doses, 5 years, minus $2B trial cost).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the main pros and cons of pricing Cortexiphan for aspergillosis at a premium vs. a discount to the market?

categories.name: Premium Pricing - Pros
ideas: Signals superior clinical profile to the market, consistent with the drug's efficacy advantage
Higher revenue per dose increases profit margin
Ability to selectively offer discounts to specific hospitals without permanently sacrificing price
Builds brand equity and pricing precedent for future indications

categories.name: Premium Pricing - Cons
ideas: Worse formulary status and lower market share than parity or discount
Bad publicity given current media and government pressure on high drug prices
May face formulary restrictions that limit physician access to the drug

categories.name: Discount Pricing - Pros
ideas: High market share and quicker product uptake
Can take price increases over time once formulary status is established
Competitive threat to existing players on price

categories.name: Discount Pricing - Cons
ideas: Decreased revenue per dose reduces profit margin
Pricing choice for aspergillosis could hinder pricing potential for rare molds or candidiasis if Massive Dynamic pursues those indications later, because a low price becomes the market expectation

recommendation: Pursue the aspergillosis indication at a premium price of $15 per dose

This strategy yields the highest risk-adjusted 5-year expected profit, estimated at approximately $28B after trial costs, driven by Cortexiphan's superior efficacy profile and the price-volume trade-off favouring premium pricing in this indication
risks: There is a 50% probability that the Phase III trial fails, which would result in a $2B loss equal to the trial cost
Premium pricing results in worse formulary status for some hospitals, limiting access and market share
Government and media pressure on pharmaceutical pricing could create reputational or regulatory risk
next_steps: Initiate Phase III clinical trial for the aspergillosis indication
Develop a hospital sales and formulary access strategy to mitigate restrictions at the $15 price point
Monitor Phase III trial data and prepare contingency plans if interim results are unfavourable
Evaluate optionality for pursuing rare molds or candidiasis indications in future if capital allows
